Polarization imaging technology can be applied to unveil the interaction between light and matter by harnessing the transverse vector wave attributes of light, thus to accentuate target characteristics amidst complex weather conditions. This technology has the potential to be widely used in road target detection. However, polarization detection is significantly affected by illumination and detection angles, as well as the considerable variation in the scale of road targets. The optimal polarization parameters should be adaptively adjusted to weather conditions, angles and target features, whereas most existing research employs handcrafted polarization parameters without considering actual complex detection requirements, which are unable to adaptively adjust the polarization feature enhancement methods. In this paper, we propose a road target detection algorithm based on an end-to-end adaptive polarization coding method, named YOLO-Polarization of Road Target Detection (YOLO-PRTD). To enhance the polarized features of targets under complex weather conditions, an Adaptive Polarization Coding Module (APCM) is designed. This module integrates channel-wise global self-attention and small kernel convolution to adaptively adjust the polarization enhancement method using dynamically extracted global and local polarization feature information. A multi-scale detection network is also designed to fully extract and fuse multi-scale feature information from receptive fields, channels, and spaces in different dimensions. Additionally, a dataset of Polarized Images of Road Targets in Complex Weather conditions (PIRT-CW) is proposed for training and evaluation. Experimental results on the PIRT-CW show that the YOLO-PRTD algorithm achieves a mAP0.5 of 89.83%, reducing the error rate by 15.54% compared to the baseline network YOLOX.

Visual perception system is a crucial component of both driving assistance and autonomous driving systems, and its performance directly affects the safety of driving systems1. In adverse weather conditions such as poor illumination, strong reflection, rain, and fog, visible images have low signal-to-noise ratio, leading to serious issues of missed and false detections by detection algorithms2. Moreover, during high-speed driving, dynamic distance changes between targets and vehicles, as well as occlusion situations, cause significant variations in target size, further increasing the challenge for detection3. Compared to traditional intensity imaging, polarization imaging unveils the differences in polarization characteristics of reflected light between targets and their backgrounds, enabling the representation of important physical features of targets even under adverse imaging conditions, thereby mitigating the impact of adverse environmental factors4. Therefore, polarization imaging is capable of meeting the needs of round-the-clock detection in complex weather conditions within the field of autonomous driving, holding important research value and promising applications.

Current mainstream target detection algorithms based on polarization imaging usually rely on extensive prior knowledge, using manually designed polarization parameters or their fusion images, to enhance the contrast between targets and the backgrounds through specific polarization features5. However, due to the differences in environmental conditions, observation angles, and target materials, targets and backgrounds exhibit complex polarization characteristic differences in the non-elastic scattering process influenced by light6. Traditional handcrafted static representation methods struggle to capture the dynamic polarization features of targets under complex weather conditions in open scenes with stability7,8. With the development of deep learning, various polarization feature enhancement methods based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have been introduced. They utilize carefully designed polarization feature extraction factors9 and convolutional kernels5,10 to obtain more polarization feature information. The polarization feature extraction factors can capture long-range dependency relationships between features by introducing a small number of parameters, highlighting the polarization characteristic differences between targets and the background9. Appropriately designed convolutional kernels can capture pixel-level polarization features between different polarization directions, fully leveraging the local detail perception capability of CNN5,10. Although CNN can effectively extract deep-layer polarization features of targets, some multi-scale key features are easily lost during the feature transmission process due to multiple up-sampling and down-sampling operations, increasing the difficulty of detecting actual multi-scale targets11.

Research indicates that the accuracy of multi-scale target detection algorithms is influenced by target scale, with accuracy significantly decreasing when targets undergo drastic scale changes or are of small size12. To address these issues, Yuan et al.13 proposed a multi-feature pyramid network based on receptive field module, balancing local and global feature extraction and enhancing the network’s robustness to scale variations. Xu et al.14 reduced the missed detection rate of small targets and refined the receptive field of the detection layer by introducing an additional high-resolution feature map. To improve model convergence precision and reduce extra inference parameters, many models have incorporated appropriate loss functions15,16. Cheng et al.15 used Generalized Intersection over Union (GIoU) optimized loss function to reduce the missed detection rate of multi-scale targets. Similarly, Wang et al.16 replaced Intersection over Union (IoU) loss with the Smoothed Intersection over Union (SIoU) loss, improving the training speed and prediction accuracy of the network. While these methods enhance the network’s multi-scale feature extraction capabilities, the performance of existing road target detection algorithms often don’t achieve ideal performance due to variations in road scenes, weather conditions, and lighting.

Compared to traditional intensity imaging, polarization imaging can provide more stable detection in complex weather conditions, holding the potential to meet the needs of round-the-clock detection17. However, there is currently limited research on how to effectively combine polarization detection with multi-scale target detection on the road. Research on target detection algorithms based on polarization imaging has the following issues: 1. Handcrafted polarization feature enhancement methods are usually only applicable to specific scenes and have low correlation with the detection network, making it difficult to flexibly adjust feature enhancement strategies according to different requirements; 2. Most such detection methods are not specifically optimized for multi-scale feature representation, resulting in the loss of crucial multi-scale information during feature transmission; 3. Existing publicly available datasets for polarized road targets lack diversity in weather conditions and the data distribution is imbalanced, which limits the generalization ability of algorithms trained on these datasets.

To address these issues, we propose a road target detection algorithm based on adaptive polarization encoding technology under complex weather conditions, named YOLO-PRTD (YOLO-Polarization of Road Target Detection). This algorithm consists of an Adaptive Polarization Coding Module (APCM) and a multi-scale detection network, which achieves road target detection under complex weather conditions by jointly optimizing polarization feature enhancement and multi-scale target detection. The APCM is designed to dynamically manage the interaction between global and local feature information using feature extraction factors and small kernel convolutions based on the brightness, color, and weather of the input image, promoting the extraction of key polarized features. The multi-scale detection network is designed to fully exploit multi-scale target feature information by extracting and integrating features at different scales and depths. The network was trained using our self-built dataset with images from complex weather conditions. By fully leveraging the advantages of APCM and multi-scale detection network, the YOLO-PRTD algorithm can adaptively handle the multi-scale features of images in different weather conditions. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

We propose the APCM that uses the entropy difference attention mechanism’s capturing capability of global feature in guiding small kernel convolutions to adaptively focus on fine polarized pixel features, thus to alternately enhance both global and local polarized feature information. Specifically, the APCM and the multi-scale detection network are trained in an end-to-end method to learn the parameters for enhancing polarization features adaptively based on bounding box annotations.

We propose the improved YOLOX-based multi-scale detection network, incorporating a Multi-Scale Feature Enhanced Module (MFEM) to fully explore feature information across receptive fields, channels, and spaces dimensions. We introduce a Tiny Target Detection Layer (TTDL) to further efficiently aggregate multi-scale features. Finally, we adopt the Efficient Intersection over Union (EIoU) loss function to improve the localization accuracy, enhancing the network’s capability to extract multi-scale features.

We propose a dataset of Polarized Images of Road Targets in Complex Weather conditions (PIRT-CW). Compared to public datasets, this dataset further integrates our independently collected data and covers a wider range of weather categories and richer scenes, enhancing the applicability and representativeness of practical road target detection applications.

Related work

This section reviews multi-scale target detection algorithms and feature enhancement methods based on polarization imaging.

Multi-scale target detection algorithms

Multi-scale target detection is a key research direction in computer vision. It addresses detection problems with varying scales and resolutions in complex backgrounds by extracting and fusing features at multiple levels. The YOLO series methods have gained significant attention for their fast and efficient single-stage detection strategy18. They incorporate various strategies such as the decoupled head, C2f, and Generalized ELAN (GELAN) to enhance multi-scale detection capabilities. YOLOX improves the prediction accuracy of multi-scale targets by applying the Decoupled Head strategy to separate classification and regression tasks19. YOLOv8 designs the C2f module to fuse features from different depths, preserving rich gradient feature information. YOLOv9 introduces GELAN to aggregate multi-layer features, and adopts a multi-path architecture to connect features across scales, significantly enhancing the capability of expressing and fusing multi-scale features20. Additionally, researchers have further improved the performance of YOLO algorithms in multi-scale target detection by introducing measures such as attention mechanisms, receptive fields, and small target detection head. Liu et al.21 proposed an improved Path Aggregation Network (PAN) based on YOLOv5 with the utilization of a small target detection head and the Wise-IoU (WIoU) function in the post-processing stage, improving the recognition and generalization ability for different targets and small-sized traffic signs. Kang et al.22 introduced a new YOLO detector (YOLO-FA) based on fuzzy attention to reduce the uncertainty of feature maps, promoting focus on the target center and effectively improving the precision of multi-scale vehicle detection.

In addition, under different algorithm frameworks, many scholars have further demonstrated that multi-scale models can efficiently extract critical feature information in networks. Zhang et al.23 utilized modules such as multi-granularity encoder (MGE) and scale-adaptive fusion (SAF) to fully integrate global and local contextual information, avoiding the potential negative impacts of cascade learning. Zhang et al.24 designed a scale adaptability (SA) module based on standard convolution and dilated convolution, adjusting the range of the receptive fields by regulating dilation factors, thus enhancing the capacity to extract and locate detailed network features. Zhang et al.25 designed a cross-layer feature aggregation (CFA) module, which aggregates features of different scales while avoiding semantic gaps, thereby achieving accurate detection of UAV targets. Zhang et al.26 proposed a Video Semantics Encoder (VSE), using average pooling and multi-head attention mechanisms to dynamically encode video features into representations ranging from coarse to fine, effectively extracting high-value visual features. In another study, Zhang et al.27 designed a UAV detection network based on full-scale feature aggregation (FFA) and grouping feature reconstruction (GFR), aggregating feature information of all scales on the premise of retaining complete information, achieving thorough information exchange. Furthermore, Zhang et al.28 developed a Bi-directional Temporal-Spatial Feature Pyramid (BiTSFP) which aggregates detailed multi-scale spatiotemporal features, and employed an Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) mechanism to automatically learn and adjust fusion weights, thereby improving the accuracy of network detection. Ding et al.29 employed multi-scale graph convolutional networks (GCN) and CNN to extract multi-scale spectral spatial features, and used cross-entropy to interpret the feature information, predicting the label of each pixel in the spectral image. Zhang et al.30 introduced an adaptive receptive path aggregation mechanism to capture rich multi-scale feature information and the importance weights of different hop neighborhoods, effectively improving the classification accuracy of hyperspectral images.

However, most traditional detection methods based on intensity imaging exhibit poor robustness in complex weather conditions. Polarization imaging compensates for the shortcomings of intensity imaging being susceptible to imaging environment influences by utilizing the transverse vector wave characteristics of light. It holds important research value and industrial application potential.

Polarization feature enhancement methods

In adverse imaging environment with poor illumination or strong reflected light, physical characteristics such as roughness, shadows, and target contours also have differentiated effects on the polarization state of light. By processing and analyzing this information, polarization imaging can effectively highlight the feature differences between targets and backgrounds31. The primary challenge in polarization-based target detection is how to fully utilize the differences between targets and backgrounds in polarization feature, and extract the key features. Existing polarization feature enhancement methods can be broadly classified into two categories: physics-based models and data fusion approaches.

Physics-based methods typically use specific physical models, such as Stokes representation or Poincaré sphere representation, to unveil the polarization differences between targets and backgrounds and improve the detection accuracy of algorithms. Shen et al.32 observed that the horizontal component polarization intensity difference image contains more polarization information of artificial targets compared to the 45° component polarization intensity difference image. They proposed an enhanced polarization parameter image (IS) by combining the Degree of Linear Polarization (DoLP) image and the Stokes representation, which highlights the polarization characteristics of disguised artificial targets. Blin et al.33 proposed various polarization parameters from multiple perspectives, such as Stokes representation, Pauli decomposition, and Poincaré sphere representation. Through validation with their self-built dataset, they found that the direction encoding image (I) is the most effective in highlighting the polarization characteristics of road targets. However, these methods are often subject to strict physical constraints and struggle to adapt to open scenes.

Enhancement methods based on data fusion combine polarized images with designed polarization parameters or intensity images to enhance target details and highlight polarization features through information complementarity between different images. Wang et al.17 pointed out that in low-visibility road scenes, DoLP images can reflect the basic polarization features of the targets, while intensity images have better visibility under good weather conditions. Complementing the information from both types of images can achieve better detection results. Sun et al.8 proposed a polarization feature extractor that uses Angle of Polarization (AoP) and DoLP as feature extraction factors from the perspective of the polarization information distribution. The extracted polarization features are then fused with the intensity image (S0), effectively reducing the model’s false detection rate. The advantage of data fusion theory lies in its flexibility to design fusion strategies according to the scenes. However, in practical detection tasks, complex imaging environment and the diverse polarization characteristics of different targets often require different data fusion methods. Fixed fusion methods in open environment may not achieve stable detection results.

While it’s established that polarization feature enhancement strategies designed based on prior knowledge can achieve excellent performance in specific tasks. However, their enhancement effects are often less satisfactory when facing environmental changes or new detection tasks. Therefore, we use CNN to autonomously learn feature enhancement methods from the data, generating appropriate polarization-enhanced images adaptively for different scenarios.

Proposed method

The proposed YOLO-PRTD is based on the YOLOX19 detection algorithm. As shown in Fig. 1, I, composed of images with polarization directions of 0°, 45°, and 90°, is used as input. The APCM fully extracts the latent polarized feature information from the images, generating adaptive polarization coded images with the enhanced information. Then, these images are fed into a multi-scale detection network for target detection.

The structure of our proposed YOLO-PRTD.

As shown in Fig. 1, the multi-scale detection network utilizes modules such as CSPLayer, SPPF, and Resblock body for feature extraction and fusion. The CSPLayer divides the input feature into two streams: one is processed through a 1 × 1 convolution layer and multiple Bottleneck modules to extract deep semantic features, while the other undergoes a direct 1 × 1 convolution layer aimed at capturing positioning features. The features from both streams are then concatenated in the channel dimension and fused via another 1 × 1 convolution layer. This approach aims to integrate features of varying depths and positions, while reducing computational load and memory consumption, thereby enhancing the model’s expressive capability; The Spatial Pyramid Pooling Fast (SPPF) structure reduces the number of channels through a 1 × 1 convolution layer, then obtains multi-scale features through multiple serial max pooling operations. The multi-scale features are concatenated with the original feature, and another 1 × 1 convolution layer is used to fuse the features, enhancing the model’s multi-scale representation capability. The Decode Predictions module extracts the key feature through shared convolutional layers. It is divided into two branches: classification and regression, which are used to predict the category of the object, whether it contains targets, and its bounding box location, respectively.

Adaptive polarization coding module (APCM)

According to the principle of focal plane imaging, the raw polarization images obtained by a focal plane polarization camera can be decomposed into four different intensity information of polarization directions: 0°, 45°, 90°, and 135°. The PEU finely explores the polarization features through small kernel convolutions. Although small kernel convolutions have good feature modeling and detail perception capabilities, enabling dynamic interaction and reorganization of pixel-level features, they may lack breadth in feature extraction. Therefore, the ESAM is further introduced, which utilizes information entropy and standard deviation as global polarization feature descriptors to comprehensively evaluate the spatial characteristics of the polarization parameter feature map, achieving weighted focus on key features. The PEU consists of three core layers: 1 × 1 convolutional layer, Silu activation layer34, and Batch Normalization layer (BN)35. The 1 × 1 convolutional layer is used for pixel-level linear operations to learn crucial pixel features between different polarization directions in polarization images. The Silu activation layer introduces non-linear operation, adding necessary complexity to the network to describe and simulate complex feature interactions. Finally, the BN layer stabilizes the output distribution of intermediate layers, reduces internal covariate shift, effectively enhances gradient stability, and accelerates the network convergence. Theoretically, the network’s ability to aggregate different features will increase with the depth36,37. However, such expansions inevitably lead to exponential increase in computational complexity and may cause gradient vanishing or explosion, thus compromising training efficiency and stability38. Therefore, referring to the network capacity design of polarization-parameter-constructing network, the number of PEUs is set to 4, and the output channel numbers are set to 8, 16, 8, and 3 respectively, as shown in Fig. 1. This configuration facilitates the deep extraction of target polarization feature information in the early stage of feature fitting, further dimension reduction in subsequent processing, while retaining key polarization feature information and reducing redundant information. Additionally, the final output channel number of the adaptive polarization coded images is set to 3, consistent with traditional RGB images, to better combine existing detection algorithms designed based on visible light images with adaptive polarization coded images, improving the accuracy of target detection.

Multi-scale feature enhanced module (MFEM)

The Focus operation with convolutional down-sampling is replaced with a designed MFEM. As shown in Fig. 3, MFEM consists of Receptive Field Block (RFB) and Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM)39. The RFB adopts a multi-scale receptive field strategy to capture extensive contextual information, reducing the impact of the Focus operation on gray-level gradient changes at the edges where the target intersects with the background. It enhances the discriminability of small targets in complex backgrounds and reduces the additional parameter overheads by adjusting channels40,41. The CBAM further enhances the network’s ability to extract multi-scale features in both spatial and channel dimensions.

The Structure of our proposed multi-scale feature enhanced module (MFEM).

The RFM employs different scales of convolutional kernels in each branch to form a multi-branch receptive field structure, improving the network’s ability to extract multi-scale features. To reduce parameter overhead, the four branches of RFM first compress the channel dimensions of the input feature map, using 1 × 1 convolutions. Three of these branches undergo 3 × 3 serial convolution operations to extract rich multi-scale features with smaller parameter overhead. The fourth branch adopts a residual structure to preserve the original key feature information of the targets. Tiny target detection layer (TTDL)

The shallow features of CNN are rich in spatial details like textures and edges, which are helpful for targets localization but lack semantic information. Deep features have richer semantic information but lack features that unveil spatial details. To improve the detection accuracy of small targets, we adopt an augmented feature fusion method. The YOLOX model obtains a series of feature maps through the backbone network for feature extraction, with their spatial resolution gradually decreasing by half while the number of features doubles. Although the feature map with the highest resolution contains the most detailed target position information, it also contains a high level of noise and background information. As shown in the red box in Fig. 1, in order to fully utilize the advanced semantic information of the low-resolution feature map, the second highest-resolution feature map is introduced into the Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN). Through the top-down feature fusion method, the advanced semantic information of the underlying low-resolution feature maps is transmitted to the high-resolution feature maps, thereby enhancing the network’s semantic understanding ability of multi-scale features. In addition, the feature maps enhanced by aggregation convey spatial detail characteristic information through a bottom-up aggregation approach, further enhancing the network’s localization capability.

In the original YOLOX network, the grid scale used for target detection is difficult to effectively cover multi-scale targets. Based on the original network’s three detection layers, we further introduce a small target detection layer with a resolution of 160 × 160 to expand the receptive field scale range of the detection layer and improve the algorithm’s small target detection accuracy.

We used Windows 10 with an AMD Ryzen 5700X processor, 16 GB of RAM and an NVIDIA Geforce GTX3080 graphics card with 10 GB of Graphics memory as the training platform. Under adverse weather conditions such as strong light, rain, fog, or poor illumination, variations in lighting and aerosol particles significantly affect the feature representation of targets in images50. When light illuminates metallic surfaces, such as cars and bikes, the surfaces typically exhibit high reflectivity and smoothness, resulting in significant specular reflections, while person, composed of rougher and lower reflectance materials such as clothing and skin, makes it challenging to capture their features8,9. Additionally, person have smaller scales compared to cars and bikes, and their shapes are more variable and prone to occlusion, further increasing detection difficulty51. In contrast, YOLO-PRTD, through the joint detection network of APCM and multi-scale detection, improves the feature representation capability by adaptively learning and enhancing the image quality through joint losses. It effectively extracts and aggregates multi-scale feature information from different receptive fields, channels, and spatial dimensions. By fully utilizing multi-scale and polarization feature information, it significantly reduces the probabilities of false positives and negatives, enhancing the network’s detection accuracy and recall rate. This meets the requirements for multi-scale and all-weather detection in complex traffic environments.

Based on this, TTDL, EIoU, and MFEM were introduced sequentially, resulting in an mAP0.5 of 89.58%, reducing the error rates by 5.58%, 8.91%, and 12.67% compared to the YOLOX baseline network, with only a slight increase in parameters of 0.9 MB and a 36.1G increase in FLOPs. In specific scenarios with complex backgrounds and dense small targets, the original YOLOX network may experience limitations and lead to missed and false detections16. Expanding the receptive field scope, extending the feature fusion range, and improving anchor box localization accuracy can enhance the discriminability and robustness of multi-scale features55,56. Conclusion

An end-to-end road target detection method YOLO-PRTD is proposed, which enhances performance under complex weather conditions through polarization feature adaptive enhancement and multi-scale feature reinforcement. The polarization feature adaptive enhancement method, enhances polarization features guided by the network’s detection requirements to suppress interference from adverse conditions. The multi-scale feature reinforcement combines multiple strategies such as TTDL, EIoU, and MFEM to extract and fuse multi-scale feature information effectively. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed YOLO-PRTD road target detection algorithm achieves stable detection performance under complex weather, with a mAP0.5 of 89.83%. Compared to the benchmark algorithm YOLOX, the error rate is reduced by 15.44%. Additionally, the proposed polarization feature enhancement method effectively handles polarization images under adverse weather conditions, achieving improvements of 48.44% and 20.98% in detection performance compared to S0 under good and adverse weather conditions, respectively.

Our experiments were conducted only in the vicinity of university campuses and common weather conditions (sunny, cloudy, foggy, evening, and rainy), which may limit the representativeness of the data in capturing real road scenes. We will consider incorporating a wider range of weather conditions and scenes in the dataset to more accurately simulate road situations in real open environments, providing data support for the integration of polarization imaging technology into autonomous driving systems.
